The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "Sizing Chaos": https://pudding.cool/2026/02/womens-sizing/
The files: data/ASTMsizes.csv, data/waistlines.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data files and reading the story.

Sizing chaos
Tip
#
# m e e t y o u r t y p i c a l
Like many girls her age, she loves to keep up with the latest fashion trends and explore new ways to express herself. Shopping is fun, but it won’t always be this way.
Scroll
“Junior’s” clothing lines often channel tweens’ interests with youthful styles that fit young girls as they grow.
For now, our typical (or median) 11-year-old wears a size 9 in the junior’s section, which is also considered a size Medium .
But not all tweens wear the same size.
If we were to look at a sample of all 10- and 11-year-old girls in the U.S. from the National Center for Health Statistics, here are the junior’s sizes that match up with their waistline measurements.
By age 15 , most girls have gone through growth spurts and puberty, and they’ve reached their adult height.
Many have started to outgrow the junior’s size section.
This marks an important turning point as they shift into women’s sizes.
Girls who fall along the bottom 10th percentile can now wear an Extra Small in women’s clothing, while girls near the 90th percentile will find that an Extra Large generally fits.
The median 15-year-old wears a Medium, as she has throughout most of her childhood.
This means for the first time ever, most girls in their cohort will be able to find a size in the women’s clothing section.
This will also likely be the last time this ever happens in their lives.
# f i t 4 a
By Amanda Sakuma
with Jan Diehm
I remember once being that teen girl shopping in the women’s section for the first time. I took stacks upon stacks of jeans with me to the dressing room, searching in vain for that one pair that fit perfectly. Over 20 years later, my hunt for the ideal pair of jeans continues. But now as an adult, I’m stuck with the countless ways that women’s apparel is not made for the average person, like me.
Children’s clothing sizes are often tied to a kid’s age or stage of development. The idea is that as a young person grows older, her clothes will evolve with her. Youth styles tend to be boxy and oversized to allow room for kids to move and grow. By early adolescence, apparel for girls becomes more fitted. Junior’s styles have higher waistlines and less-pronounced curves compared to adult clothing lines. In short: clothes for tweens are made for tween bodies.
By the time most teenage girls can wear women’s clothes — around age 15 — their options are seemingly endless. But the evolution in clothing sizes that followed girls throughout childhood abruptly stops there.
This is the reality I find myself reckoning with today: Women’s clothing — designed for adults — fits modern teen girls better.
Age: 14-15
Sizes: Women's
Waistline in Inches
At age 15 a size Medium still equals the median waistline but, from here on, the two will diverge.
In addition to generic letter sizes (Small, Medium, Large etc.), women have a numeric sizing system that is designed to be more tailored and precise. Here, the median 15-year-old’s waistline fits a size 10 .
The median 20-something will eventually move up a letter size to a Large .
In U.S. women’s sizing, this translates to a size 14 .
Her wardrobe will shift again in her 30s.
At this point the median woman is closer to a size 16 or Extra Large.
This trend will continue again, and again.
Altogether, the median adult woman over the age of 20 fits a size 18.
The problem is that most “Straight” or “Regular” size ranges only go up to a size 16.
That leaves millions of people — over half of all adult women — who are excluded from standard size ranges.
# P a i n i s
s i z i n g i s n o t
Few life experiences feel as universal, across generations, as the pains and frustrations of trying to find clothes that fit.
Sizes vary wildly from store to store. Even within a single apparel company, no one size is consistent. There are no regulations or universal sizing standards. Instead each brand is incentivized to make up its own. When size guides change — and they’re always changing — brands are not obligated to disclose updates.
There are also often different sizing structures for every type of garment. “Plus” size means one thing, “curve” means another, and “extended” sizes can be defined as all of the above or something else entirely. Don’t count on any of those sizes to be available to try on in-store, but do brace for return fees if your online order doesn’t fit. Free in-store alterations are largely a thing of the past, while a trip to the tailor’s can cost just as much as the item itself.
The only consistent feature is that the industry at large continues to cling onto the same underlying sizing system that’s been broken for decades. And it’s only gotten worse.

While there are no universal sizing standards, an organization called ASTM International regularly releases informal guidelines.
Here, each current ASTM size (00–20) is represented by a dot.
Clothing manufacturers may loosely follow those standards, but more often than not, brands prefer to tailor their own practices to their target customer base.
These dots represent the size charts of 15 popular brands. Dots connected by a shaded background show when measurements or sizes are presented as a range.
Sizes are frequently inconsistent and undefined.
Generic letter sizes often group multiple numeric sizes together, with no universal standard for what “Small” or “Medium” actually means. For example, here’s every size that is labeled as Large , spanning waistlines from 29 to 34 inches.
Here is our median 15-year-old girl in the U.S. With a waistline measuring 30.4 inches, she fits around a size 10 according to ASTM standards.
While it’s unlikely that clothing designed for adults will fit a teen’s body perfectly, she has quite a few sizing options.
However as she’ll quickly learn, sizes are not universal across all brands. Here are all the sizes within 1 inch of the median teen’s waistline.
At Reformation, she’s closer to a size 8. At Uniqlo, she’s considered a size 12.
The median adult woman has a much harder time finding clothes that fit. Her waistline is 37.68 inches, placing her at a size 18 by ASTM standards.
Many brands don’t carry her size. This is especially true for high-end, luxury fashion labels.
Sizing issues are amplified even further within Plus size ranges. Some Plus sizes start at size 12, others at 18. Others still consider any size from 00 to 30 as part of their Regular line.
The median adult woman may also find herself in what’s informally called the “mid-size gap,” seen here in Anthropologie’s size chart.
Sizes within the Regular size range are too small, yet the next size up in the Plus range might be too big.
Even the symbols used to describe certain sizes hold a wide range of meanings.
For the average adult woman, there are as many as 10 different ways to describe the garments that she could conceivably wear from these brands alone. At Reformation she’s closer to a size 14. At Shein, she’s a 2XL in their plus size range.
Explore more
Interact with the dots for more information about each brand and size.
# T h e v i l l a i n a r c o f
On top of all these problems, consumers often know the labels for any given size cannot be trusted.
Vanity sizing, the practice where size labels stay the same even as the underlying measurements frequently become larger, is so ubiquitous across the fashion and apparel industry that younger generations have never experienced a world without it.
Cultural narratives around vanity sizing often square the blame on female shoppers, not brands. Newsweek once called it “self-delusion on a mass scale” because women were more likely to buy items that were labeled as sizes smaller than reality. But there’s more to the story.
Vanity sizing provides a powerful marketing strategy for brands. Companies found that whenever women needed a size larger than expected, they were less likely to follow through on their purchases. Some could even develop negative associations with the brand and never shop there again. But when manufacturers manipulated sizing labels, leading to a more positive customer experience, brands could maintain a slight competitive edge.
The dynamic perpetuates an arms race toward artificially deflating size labels. Most shoppers aren’t even aware when size charts change, or by how much. If anything, vanity sizing consistently gaslights women to the point where few are able to know their “true” size. But where would we be today without it?

It’s true: Sizes today are much larger than they were in the past.
Roughly 30 years ago, ASTM guidelines covered waistlines between 24 and 36.5 inches, representing a 12.5-inch spread from size 2–20. (While extended sizes technically existed at the time, they were not widely available in stores).
In the early 2000s ASTM added size 00 and 0 to pad out the bottom of the range.
Today, because of vanity sizing, we can see an upward shift in all sizes. ASTM guidelines span 15.12 inches from 25.38–40.5 inches for sizes 00–20.
By comparison, today’s size 8 is 2.5 inches larger in the waist than it was 30 years ago.
But vanity sizing didn’t just account for women’s unconscious shopping behaviors. Clothes needed to be larger because our waistlines had grown.
The average woman’s waistline today is nearly 4 inches wider than it was in the mid-1990s.
Here’s the surprising silver lining to vanity sizing: Over this 30-year period, the median adult woman has almost always fit the size 18 that was available to her at the time.
Vanity sizing has effectively helped manufacturers keep up to pace with demographic shifts in the U.S. But only for the smallest half of all adult women.
Explore more
Interact with the dress forms to see how sizes changed from 1995 to 2021.
#
I once believed that change was inevitable and sizing problems would become a relic of the past. If it wasn’t some scrappy upstart that promised to revolutionize the sizing system, then at least the major fashion conglomerates would be well-placed to modernize and tap the full potential of the plus-size market. But that progress never fully materialized. And I got tired of waiting.
A few years ago, I started learning how to sew. Somehow it felt more practical to make my own clothes than count on meaningful change to happen on its own. Getting started was easier than I thought. The first sewing pattern I ever completed — a boxy, drop-shoulder style that could turn into either a shirt or dress — was free to download. It included a 29-page instruction manual with photos and illustrations documenting every step.
Drafting a custom pattern based on my body measurements and proportions
From there, I started learning how to draft my own sewing patterns from scratch. That’s when I realized the truth behind my sizing struggles: Clothing sizes are optimized for mass production and appeal — not women’s bodies. Nothing represents this more than a size 8.
Fashion designers often use body measurements for a size 8 as a starting point when creating new design samples. Manufacturers then use a mathematical formula to determine each next size up or down the range in a process called grading. The effect is like a Russian doll. Each size up is incrementally larger than the last.
The uniform shape makes it easier for factories to mass-produce garments, however it comes with several tradeoffs. It’s hard to scale up to larger-sized clothing before the proportions become distorted. It also becomes impractical to make multiple versions of a single item to accommodate varying body shapes or heights. That means most women’s clothing is derived from a single set of proportions — a size 8. According to U.S. health data, fewer than 10% of adult women have waistlines that fit the standard sample size or smaller.
I, like the vast majority of women, do not fit the standard mold. Instead I took an old pattern-making textbook often taught in fashion design schools to start making clothes to fit my own unique proportions. I gathered and recorded over 58 different body measurements in order to get started and from there, I could make my own custom base pattern, known as a bodice block or sloper.
Standard bodice block
My bodice block
Once I compared my personalized sloper to commercial patterns and retail garments, I had a revelation: clothes were never made to fit bodies like mine. It didn’t matter how much weight I gained or lost, whether I contorted my body or tried to buy my way into styles that “flatter” my silhouette, there was no chance that clothes would ever fit perfectly on their own. Finally I understood why.
Inverted Triangle
Top Hourglass

As women, it’s drilled into our heads that the ideal body type is the hourglass: wide shoulders and hips and a snatched waist.
But that’s an unrealistic standard for most people.
Researchers have identified as many as nine different categories of body proportions commonly found among adult women alone. Many are likely familiar to those told over the years to “dress for their body type.”
Most women do not have an exaggerated hourglass silhouette, instead the median woman is shaped more like a rectangle.
That’s because age and race factor heavily into how our bodies are shaped. Genetics can influence everything from a person's proportions to how they build muscle mass to where their bodies tend to store fat.
One 2007 study found that half of women (49%) in the U.S. were considered rectangle-shaped. Only 12% of women had a true hourglass figure.
While the U.S. does not track bust measurements,* we know that the median woman's waist-to-hip difference is roughly half that of 'ideal' hourglass proportions.
Still, size charts continue to champion a defined waistline as the sole foundation to most women’s apparel.
For example, here’s J.Crew’s size chart. They use a rigid set of dimensions, where the waist measurement is exactly 10 inches smaller than the hip for all sizes.
That means the smallest and largest sizes in a range will have the exact same body shape.
Actual bodies, however, are far less uniform or symmetrical.
A size 18 pair of pants from J.Crew might fit the median woman’s waist, but they’d likely be too large in the hips by at least 6 inches.
Conversely a size 12 would fit her hips best, but it’s unlikely that she’d be able to squeeze into a waistband that’s 6 inches smaller than her own.
Of course, J. Crew isn’t the only brand whose size chart is distorted. It’s the industry standard.
Out of these 15 brands, only H&M comes close to the median woman’s shape, especially as sizes get bigger.
Explore more
Use the selector in the top left corner, to highlight a size.
# s i z i n g f o r
The fashion industry thrives on exclusivity. Luxury brands maintain their status by limiting who is able to buy or even wear their clothes. If few women fit the “ideal” standards, then products serving only them are inherently exclusionary. Size charts become the de facto dividing line determining who belongs and who doesn’t.
This line of gatekeeping is baked into the foundation of virtually all clothing. The modern sizing system in the U.S. was developed in the 1940s based on mostly young, white women. No women of color were originally included. The system was never built to include a diverse cross-section of people, ages, or body types. It has largely stayed that way by design.
In its 1995 standards update, ASTM International admitted that its sizing guidelines were never meant to represent the population at large. Instead body measurements were based on “designer experience” and “market observations.” The goal was to tailor sizes to the existing customer base. But what happens when more than half of all women are pushed to the margins or left behind?
It doesn’t have to be this way. Teenage girls shouldn’t be aging out of sizing options from the moment they start wearing women’s clothes. A woman does not need hourglass proportions to look good, just as garment-makers do not need standardized sizes to produce well-fitting clothes.
There are no rules forcing brands to adopt any particular sizing system. There is no such thing as a “true” size 8, or any size for that matter. If brands are constantly developing and customizing their size charts, then it makes little sense to perpetuate a broken system. Sizes are all made up anyway — why can’t we make them better?
# Methodology
To highlight the median body proportions of the adult women in the U.S., we relied on anthropometric reference data for children and adults that is regularly released by the National Center for Health Statistics within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
For this story, we pulled data on the median waistline circumference of women and girls that was gathered between 2021-2023 . For girls and women under 20 years old, measurements were recorded in two-year age ranges (ex: 10–11 years, 14–15 years), with a median of 141 participants per age range. For women over 20, measurements were recorded in nine-year age ranges (ex: 20–29 years, 30–39 years) and collectively for all women 20 and older. Each nine-year age range had a median of 465 participants. Overall, measurements were recorded for 3,121 women ages 20 and older. Those who were pregnant were excluded from the data.
HHS also provides a breakdown of measurements within set percentiles for each age range, which includes figures for the 5th, 10th, 15th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 85th, 90th, and 95th percentiles. We then used that percentile data to extrapolate the waistline measurements of all women and girls within each respective age group.
We also compared figures to those recorded by HHS from 1988-1994 . There, 7,410 women ages 20 and older participated in the study. Measurements were originally recorded in centimeters, so we converted to inches.
Brands included in the size chart comparisons represent a diverse cross-section of popular apparel brands and retailers in the U.S., including a mix of mass market, fast fashion, premium and luxury labels.
For each brand, we focused on collecting body measurements for “regular” or “standard” size ranges, as well as “plus” sizes when available. Sizing information for “petite,” “tall,” or “curve” clothing lines were not included. Size charts reflect the body measurements for garments categorized as general “apparel.” In a select few cases where that category was unavailable, “dresses” were used as the default garment type.
Within each size range, we focused on collecting three main body measurements: Bust, waist, and hip. Some were presented as a range from minimum to maximum values, while others were single measurements. All numeric U.S. women’s sizing labels and descriptions were recorded, as well as their corresponding alpha sizes, when available.
Size chart data was last manually captured in July 2025 and may not reflect a brand’s current size chart. Brands frequently change their size charts, and more often than not, shoppers aren’t even aware when measurements or sizes are updated.
The standardized size charts refer to ASTM International’s regular release of its Standard Table of Measurements for Adult Female Misses Figure Type. The 1995 release (designated as D 5585-95) reflects sizes 2-20. ASTM updated its standards in 2021 (designated as D5585-21 ) to include sizes 00-20.

I remember once being that teen girl shopping in the women’s section for the first time. I took stacks upon stacks of jeans with me to the dressing room, searching in vain for that one pair that fit perfectly. Over 20 years later, my hunt for the ideal pair of jeans continues. But now as an adult, I’m stuck with the countless ways that women’s apparel is not made for the average person, like me.
Children’s clothing sizes are often tied to a kid’s age or stage of development. The idea is that as a young person grows older, her clothes will evolve with her. Youth styles tend to be boxy and oversized to allow room for kids to move and grow. By early adolescence, apparel for girls becomes more fitted. Junior’s styles have higher waistlines and less-pronounced curves compared to adult clothing lines. In short: clothes for tweens are made for tween bodies.
By the time most teenage girls can wear women’s clothes — around age 15 — their options are seemingly endless. But the evolution in clothing sizes that followed girls throughout childhood abruptly stops there.
This is the reality I find myself reckoning with today: Women’s clothing — designed for adults — fits modern teen girls better.

Few life experiences feel as universal, across generations, as the pains and frustrations of trying to find clothes that fit.
Sizes vary wildly from store to store. Even within a single apparel company, no one size is consistent. There are no regulations or universal sizing standards. Instead each brand is incentivized to make up its own. When size guides change — and they’re always changing — brands are not obligated to disclose updates.
There are also often different sizing structures for every type of garment. “Plus” size means one thing, “curve” means another, and “extended” sizes can be defined as all of the above or something else entirely. Don’t count on any of those sizes to be available to try on in-store, but do brace for return fees if your online order doesn’t fit. Free in-store alterations are largely a thing of the past, while a trip to the tailor’s can cost just as much as the item itself.
The only consistent feature is that the industry at large continues to cling onto the same underlying sizing system that’s been broken for decades. And it’s only gotten worse.

On top of all these problems, consumers often know the labels for any given size cannot be trusted.
Vanity sizing, the practice where size labels stay the same even as the underlying measurements frequently become larger, is so ubiquitous across the fashion and apparel industry that younger generations have never experienced a world without it.
Cultural narratives around vanity sizing often square the blame on female shoppers, not brands.
Newsweek
once called it “self-delusion on a mass scale” because women were more likely to buy items that were labeled as sizes smaller than reality. But there’s more to the story.
Vanity sizing provides a powerful
marketing strategy
for brands. Companies found that whenever women needed a size larger than expected, they were less likely to follow through on their purchases. Some could even develop negative associations with the brand and never shop there again. But when manufacturers manipulated sizing labels, leading to a more positive customer experience, brands could maintain a slight competitive edge.
The dynamic perpetuates an arms race toward artificially deflating size labels. Most shoppers aren’t even aware when size charts change, or by how much. If anything, vanity sizing consistently gaslights women to the point where few are able to know their “true” size. But where would we be today without it?

I once believed that change was inevitable and sizing problems would become a relic of the past. If it wasn’t some scrappy upstart that promised to revolutionize the sizing system, then at least the major fashion conglomerates would be well-placed to modernize and tap the full potential of the plus-size market. But that progress never fully materialized. And I got tired of waiting.
A few years ago, I started learning how to sew. Somehow it felt more practical to make my own clothes than count on meaningful change to happen on its own. Getting started was easier than I thought. The first sewing pattern I ever completed — a boxy, drop-shoulder style that could turn into either a shirt or dress — was free to download. It included a 29-page instruction manual with photos and illustrations documenting every step.
Drafting a custom pattern based on my body measurements and proportions
From there, I started learning how to draft my own sewing patterns from scratch. That’s when I realized the truth behind my sizing struggles: Clothing sizes are optimized for mass production and appeal — not women’s bodies. Nothing represents this more than a size 8.
Fashion designers often use body measurements for a
as a starting point when creating new design samples. Manufacturers then use a mathematical formula to determine each next size up or down the range in a process called grading. The effect is like a Russian doll. Each size up is incrementally larger than the last.
The uniform shape makes it easier for factories to mass-produce garments, however it comes with several tradeoffs. It’s hard to scale up to larger-sized clothing before the proportions become distorted. It also becomes impractical to make multiple versions of a single item to accommodate varying body shapes or heights. That means most women’s clothing is derived from a single set of proportions — a size 8. According to U.S. health data, fewer than 10% of adult women have waistlines that fit the standard sample size or smaller.
I, like the vast majority of women, do not fit the standard mold. Instead I took an old pattern-making textbook often taught in fashion design schools to start making clothes to fit my own unique proportions. I gathered and recorded over 58 different body measurements in order to get started and from there, I could make my own
custom base pattern,
known as a bodice block or sloper.
Standard bodice block
My bodice block
Once I compared my personalized sloper to commercial patterns and retail garments, I had a revelation: clothes were never made to fit bodies like mine. It didn’t matter how much weight I gained or lost, whether I contorted my body or tried to buy my way into styles that “flatter” my silhouette, there was no chance that clothes would ever fit perfectly on their own. Finally I understood why.

As women, it’s drilled into our heads that the ideal body type is the hourglass: wide shoulders and hips and a snatched waist.
But that’s an unrealistic standard for most people.
Researchers
have identified as many as nine different categories of body proportions commonly found among adult women alone. Many are likely familiar to those told over the years to “dress for their body type.”
Most women do not have an exaggerated hourglass silhouette, instead the
median woman
is shaped more like a rectangle.
That’s because age and race factor heavily into how our bodies are shaped. Genetics can influence everything from a person's proportions to how they build muscle mass to where their bodies tend to store fat.
One 2007
study
found that half of women (49%) in the U.S. were considered rectangle-shaped. Only 12% of women had a true hourglass figure.
While the U.S. does not track bust measurements,* we know that the
median woman's
waist-to-hip difference is roughly half that of
'ideal' hourglass proportions.
Still, size charts continue to champion a defined waistline as the sole foundation to most women’s apparel.
For example, here’s J.Crew’s size chart. They use a rigid set of dimensions, where the waist measurement is exactly
10 inches smaller
than the hip for all sizes.
That means the smallest and largest sizes in a range will have the exact same body shape.
Actual bodies, however, are far less uniform or symmetrical.
A
pair of pants from J.Crew might fit the median woman’s waist, but they’d likely be too large in the hips by at least 6 inches.
Conversely a
size 12
would fit her hips best, but it’s unlikely that she’d be able to squeeze into a waistband that’s 6 inches smaller than her own.
Highlight
Of course, J. Crew isn’t the only brand whose size chart is distorted. It’s the industry standard.
Out of these 15 brands, only H&M comes close to the median woman’s shape, especially as sizes get bigger.
Use the selector in the top left corner, to highlight a size.
The fashion industry thrives on exclusivity. Luxury brands maintain their status by limiting who is able to buy or even wear their clothes. If few women fit the “ideal” standards, then products serving only them are inherently exclusionary. Size charts become the de facto dividing line determining who belongs and who doesn’t.
This line of gatekeeping is baked into the foundation of virtually all clothing. The modern sizing system in the U.S. was
developed in the 1940s
based on mostly young, white women. No women of color were originally included. The system was never built to include a diverse cross-section of people, ages, or body types. It has largely stayed that way by design.
In its 1995 standards update, ASTM International admitted that its sizing guidelines were never meant to represent the population at large. Instead body measurements were based on “designer experience” and “market observations.” The goal was to tailor sizes to the existing customer base. But what happens when more than half of all women are pushed to the margins or left behind?
It doesn’t have to be this way. Teenage girls shouldn’t be aging out of sizing options from the moment they start wearing women’s clothes. A woman does not need hourglass proportions to look good, just as garment-makers do not need standardized sizes to produce well-fitting clothes.
There are no rules forcing brands to adopt any particular sizing system. There is no such thing as a “true” size 8, or any size for that matter. If brands are constantly developing and customizing their size charts, then it makes little sense to perpetuate a broken system. Sizes are all made up anyway — why can’t we make them better?
Methodology
To highlight the median body proportions of the adult women in the U.S., we relied on anthropometric reference data for children and adults that is regularly released by the National Center for Health Statistics within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
For this story, we pulled data on the median waistline circumference of women and girls that was
gathered between 2021-2023
. For girls and women under 20 years old, measurements were recorded in two-year age ranges (ex: 10–11 years, 14–15 years), with a median of 141 participants per age range. For women over 20, measurements were recorded in nine-year age ranges (ex: 20–29 years, 30–39 years) and collectively for all women 20 and older. Each nine-year age range had a median of 465 participants. Overall, measurements were recorded for 3,121 women ages 20 and older. Those who were pregnant were excluded from the data.
HHS also provides a breakdown of measurements within set percentiles for each age range, which includes figures for the 5th, 10th, 15th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 85th, 90th, and 95th percentiles. We then used that percentile data to extrapolate the waistline measurements of all women and girls within each respective age group.
We also compared figures to those recorded by HHS from
1988-1994
. There, 7,410 women ages 20 and older participated in the study. Measurements were originally recorded in centimeters, so we converted to inches.
Brands included in the size chart comparisons represent a diverse cross-section of popular apparel brands and retailers in the U.S., including a mix of mass market, fast fashion, premium and luxury labels.
For each brand, we focused on collecting body measurements for “regular” or “standard” size ranges, as well as “plus” sizes when available. Sizing information for “petite,” “tall,” or “curve” clothing lines were not included. Size charts reflect the body measurements for garments categorized as general “apparel.” In a select few cases where that category was unavailable, “dresses” were used as the default garment type.
Within each size range, we focused on collecting three main body measurements: Bust, waist, and hip. Some were presented as a range from minimum to maximum values, while others were single measurements. All numeric U.S. women’s sizing labels and descriptions were recorded, as well as their corresponding alpha sizes, when available.
Size chart data was last manually captured in July 2025 and may not reflect a brand’s current size chart. Brands frequently change their size charts, and more often than not, shoppers aren’t even aware when measurements or sizes are updated.
The standardized size charts refer to ASTM International’s regular release of its Standard Table of Measurements for Adult Female Misses Figure Type. The 1995 release (designated as D 5585-95) reflects sizes 2-20. ASTM updated its standards in 2021 (designated as
D5585-21
) to include sizes 00-20.

"""Write down a Pudding story's findings, as facts, with a pi agent that reads the story on the web.

    PYTHONPATH=src:../report-bench/src .venv/bin/python -m report_gepa.originals <out_dir> [id ...] [--workers 8] [--model m]

These are the answers for rubric 2.1 (finding coverage): the findings the
original's authors drew from the task's data, written the way a page's
facts.json is (report-bench/TASK.md), so a page's facts can be matched against
them. Without ids, every task with an original.json in report-bench/out/answers.

The agent (agent/gen.mjs with WEB_TOOLS=1) gets the task's data under data/ and
the story's address. It reads the story with web_fetch and web_view (agent/web.mjs,
run outside the sandbox), lists every finding the authors state or label, and
writes the ones the data reproduces as facts, each quoting the story's words in
`source`; the rest go to skipped.json with the reason. Then every fact is run
again and its claim read against its printout, as trust.py does for a page (1.2,
1.3), and its source looked up in the text the agent's web tools returned. The
facts that pass are the answer, answer.json; the others are listed in
record.json under `dropped`. Each task lives in <out_dir>/<id>/: facts.json (the
agent's), answer.json, skipped.json, record.json and session.jsonl; the copied
data is removed afterwards. A task whose answer.json exists is skipped, so a
stopped run picks up where it was. With --answers, answer.json is also copied to
report-bench/out/answers/<id>/facts.json.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import html
import json
import os
import re
import shutil
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

from report_bench.llm import OutOfCredit, credit_refused
from report_bench.trust import claims_hold, run_facts

from .generate import GEN_MODEL, ROOT, run_agent

BENCH = ROOT.parent / "report-bench" / "out"

SYSTEM = """You are a careful data analyst. You read a published data story and write down, as checkable facts, the findings its authors drew from their data. You quote the story exactly, you compute every number from the files you are given, and you never type a number into code. You work in English."""

TASK = """The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "{title}": {url}
The files: {files}

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {{"m": "data/measurements.csv"}},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
"""


def task_text(task_id: str) -> str:
    original = json.loads((BENCH / "answers" / task_id / "original.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    task = json.loads((BENCH / "tasks" / task_id / "task.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return TASK.format(title=original["title"], url=original["url"], files=", ".join(task["files"]))


def _norm(s: str) -> str:
    # web_fetch leaves entities such as ‘ undecoded, so both sides are unescaped first
    return re.sub(r"[\W_]+", " ", html.unescape(s)).lower().strip()


def quoted(source: str, read: str) -> bool:
    """Whether every part of a quote is in what was read; parts joined by an ellipsis may sit apart, as chart labels do."""
    parts = [_norm(x) for x in re.split(r"\.\.\.|\u2026", source)]
    return bool(any(parts)) and all(x in read for x in parts if x)


def read_on_web(session: Path) -> str:
    """Everything the agent's web tools returned, normalised for looking quotes up."""
    text = []
    for line in session.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        try:
            m = json.loads(line).get("message", {})
        except json.JSONDecodeError:  # a line cut off while the file was written
            continue
        if m.get("role") == "toolResult" and m.get("toolName") in ("web_fetch", "web_view"):
            text += [c.get("text", "") for c in m.get("content", []) if c.get("type") == "text"]
    return _norm(" ".join(text))


def extract(task_id: str, out_dir: Path, model: str, effort: str = "high") -> dict:
    ws = out_dir / task_id
    shutil.rmtree(ws, ignore_errors=True)
    shutil.copytree(BENCH / "tasks" / task_id / "data", ws / "data")
    task_path = out_dir / f"{task_id}.task.md"
    task_path.write_text(task_text(task_id), encoding="utf-8")
    system_path = out_dir / "system.md"
    run = run_agent(ws, system_path, model, effort, f"  {task_id}", task_path, output="facts.json")
    if credit_refused(run.get("error")):
        shutil.rmtree(ws, ignore_errors=True)
        raise OutOfCredit(run["error"])
    record = {"id": task_id, "model": model, "effort": effort, "run": run}
    data = sorted((ws / "data").iterdir())
    problems, facts, results = run_facts(ws / "facts.json", data)
    record["facts"] = len(facts)
    record["problems"] = problems
    if not facts and not problems:  # the story states nothing this data reproduces
        record["dropped"], record["answer"] = [], 0
        (ws / "answer.json").write_text("[]", encoding="utf-8")
    if facts and not problems:
        check = claims_hold(facts, results, model)
        record["wrong"] = check["wrong"]
        record["verdicts"] = check["verdicts"]
        if check["wrong"] is not None:
            read = read_on_web(ws / "session.jsonl") if (ws / "session.jsonl").exists() else ""
            wrong = {v["id"] for v in check["wrong"]}
            dropped = [{"id": f["id"], "why": "claim does not agree with its printout"} for f in facts if f["id"] in wrong]
            dropped += [{"id": f["id"], "why": "source not in the story as read"} for f in facts
                        if f["id"] not in wrong and not quoted(str(f.get("source", "")), read)]
            gone = {d["id"] for d in dropped}
            answer = [f for f in facts if f["id"] not in gone]
            record["dropped"] = dropped
            record["answer"] = len(answer)
            (ws / "answer.json").write_text(json.dumps(answer, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")
    skipped = ws / "skipped.json"
    try:
        record["skipped"] = len(json.loads(skipped.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
        record["skipped"] = None
    shutil.rmtree(ws / "data")
    (ws / "record.json").write_text(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")
    return record


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("out", type=Path)
    ap.add_argument("ids", nargs="*")
    ap.add_argument("--model", default=GEN_MODEL)
    ap.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=8)
    ap.add_argument("--answers", action="store_true", help="copy each answer.json to report-bench/out/answers/<id>/facts.json")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    ids = args.ids or sorted(p.parent.name for p in (BENCH / "answers").glob("*/original.json"))
    args.out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (args.out / "system.md").write_text(SYSTEM, encoding="utf-8")
    os.environ["WEB_TOOLS"] = "1"  # run_agent passes the environment on to gen.mjs

    def one(task_id):
        if (args.out / task_id / "answer.json").exists():  # done in an earlier run
            return
        try:
            r = extract(task_id, args.out, args.model)
        except OutOfCredit:
            raise
        except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - one task's failure is reported, not the end of the run
            print(f"{task_id}: crashed {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:200]}", flush=True)
            return
        answer = args.out / task_id / "answer.json"
        if args.answers and answer.exists():
            shutil.copy2(answer, BENCH / "answers" / task_id / "facts.json")
        print(f"{task_id}: facts={r['facts']} answer={r.get('answer')} dropped={len(r.get('dropped', []))} "
              f"skipped={r['skipped']} problems={len(r['problems'])} {r['run'].get('seconds')}s steps={r['run'].get('steps')}",
              flush=True)

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(args.workers) as pool:
        list(pool.map(one, ids))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Score a guide on the val stories of runs/gepa/full, the way GEPA scores a candidate.

    PYTHONPATH=src:../report-bench/src .venv/bin/python -m report_gepa.evalguide runs/<name> [--guide guides/seed.md] [--with-rubric]

--with-rubric appends the scoring rules the page is scored by: the trust vetoes (1.1-1.3), and every
scored item with its description, its five bands and the text of its worked
examples (the judge also sees the examples' screenshots; a guide carries only
their text). It is the baseline a judge-driven optimiser has to beat: the
writer is told the judge's standard up front. One page per val story is
written and judged by the same Adapter as GEPA's; pages and judgements go to
<run>/rollouts/<guide hash>/ and the guide to <run>/guides/.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from pathlib import Path
from statistics import mean

from .generate import GUIDES
from report_bench.judge import _item_block
from .optimize import Adapter, split
from report_bench.rubric import load

RUBRIC_HEADER = """

下面是这些网页的评分标准。每个网页由评审照这份标准打分:先看可信 1.1–1.3,犯了任何一条就整页 0 分;否则「表达」各条和「美感」各条分别打 0–1 分,总分是这些条的平均,2.2 论证和 2.3 叙事合起来算一条。"""


def rubric_text() -> str:
    rubric = load()
    parts = [f"{it.id} {it.name}(一票否决)\n说明:{it.description}" for it in rubric.values() if "门槛" in it.mode]
    for it in (r for r in rubric.values() if r.scored):
        block = _item_block(it, True)
        if it.examples:
            block += "\n典型案例:\n" + "\n".join(f"- {e.score} 分:{e.note}" for e in it.examples)
        parts.append(block)
    return RUBRIC_HEADER + "\n\n" + "\n\n".join(parts) + "\n"


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("run", type=Path)
    ap.add_argument("--guide", type=Path, default=GUIDES / "seed.md")
    ap.add_argument("--with-rubric", action="store_true", help="append the judge's scoring rules to the guide")
    ap.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=8)
    ap.add_argument("--browsers", type=int, default=4)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    guide = args.guide.read_text(encoding="utf-8") + (rubric_text() if args.with_rubric else "")
    _, val, _ = split(8, 19, 0)  # GEPA's split of runs/gepa/full
    args.run.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    adapter = Adapter(args.run, args.workers, args.browsers)
    print(f"== {args.guide.name}{' + rubric' if args.with_rubric else ''}: {len(guide)} characters, {len(val)} val stories", flush=True)
    batch = adapter.evaluate(val, {"guide": guide})
    for story, r in zip(val, batch.outputs):
        print(f"{story:18} {r['score']:.3f}  {r['summary']}", flush=True)
    print(f"val mean {mean(batch.scores):.3f}", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""The score of a page: the one definition the benchmark, GEPA and TF-GRPO share.

    PYTHONPATH=../report-gepa/src:src ../report-gepa/.venv/bin/python -m report_bench.score submissions/<system> [--tasks a,b] [--out runs/<system>] [--workers 4] [--browsers 2] | tee runs/<system>.log

score_page scores one delivered page (a folder with index.html and facts.json,
see TASK.md) made from `data`, the files and folders its writer found in data/:

1. capture: the page is captured with the data (capture.py) into <out>/evidence.
2. trust (1.x, trust.py): renders, refs hold, data accurate. Any violated item
   makes the score 0 and the page is not judged further: a page that misstates
   its data is not a better page for being clear or pretty.
3. expression (2.x) and aesthetics (3.x): 2.2 argument and 2.3 narrative from
   the page's prose, one call each (article.py); the rest from the screenshots,
   one judge call per dimension (judge.py).
4. the score: the mean of the scored items, equal weights until weights are
   fitted on whole-page labels, except that 2.2 and 2.3 count as one item
   between them (WEIGHT): together they say how the article is told.

A check that gives no usable answer (1.3 without parseable JSON, a judge call
that leaves an item without a score) is asked again, up to TRIES times in all;
the tries are kept, so a restart does not ask a hopeless page again. A page whose
checks are still missing an answer is `complete: false`: its score covers only
what was answered, and callers that compare pages (TF-GRPO) leave it out.

Everything is kept in <out>: evidence/, trust.json, judgements.json,
article.json and result.json, and reused when present, so a restart or a repeated request costs
nothing. The result's feedback lines (every trust problem, every item's score and
reason, the page's scroll facts) are what GEPA reflects on.

The benchmark command scores submissions/<system>/<id>/ for every task in
out/tasks/ with the task's data, writes <out>/scores.jsonl and prints the means by
source. A task with no page scores 0.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from contextlib import nullcontext
from pathlib import Path
from statistics import mean

from . import article as A
from . import judge as J
from . import trust as T
from .capture import capture
from .llm import OutOfCredit
from .rubric import load

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
TASKS = ROOT / "out" / "tasks"
MODEL = "deepseek-v4.1-flash"  # GEPA's and TF-GRPO's judge, so benchmark scores compare with their runs
TRIES = 3
WEIGHT = {"2.2": 0.5, "2.3": 0.5}  # argument and narrative are halves of one item; every other item weighs 1


def _read(path: Path, default):
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if path.exists() else default


def _write(path: Path, value) -> None:
    path.write_text(json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")


def _trust(page: Path, ev: Path, out: Path, model: str) -> dict:
    path = out / "trust.json"
    record = _read(path, None)
    tries = record["tries"] if record else 0
    while tries < TRIES and (record is None or record["items"].get("1.3", {}).get("violated", False) is None):
        tries += 1
        record = {**T.trust(ev, page / "facts.json", model), "tries": tries}
        if "1.3" in record["items"]:
            (out / "trust-prompt.txt").write_text(record["items"]["1.3"].pop("prompt"), encoding="utf-8")
        _write(path, record)
    return record


def _judge(ev: Path, out: Path, model: str) -> dict:
    path = out / "judgements.json"
    items = _read(path, {})
    tries = items.setdefault("tries", {})
    scored = [it for it in load().values() if it.scored and not it.prose_only]
    for dim in ([it for it in scored if it.id.startswith(d)] for d in ("2.", "3.")):
        name = dim[0].id[0] + ".x"
        while tries.get(name, 0) < TRIES and not all(items.get(it.id, {}).get("score") is not None for it in dim):
            tries[name] = tries.get(name, 0) + 1
            try:
                items.update(J.page_group(dim, ev, model)[1])
            except OutOfCredit:
                raise
            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - asked again; still missing, the page is incomplete
                print(f"[judge] {out.name} {name}: FAILED {str(e)[:200]}", flush=True)
            _write(path, items)
    return items


def _article(ev: Path, out: Path, model: str) -> dict:
    path = out / "article.json"
    items = _read(path, {})
    tries = items.setdefault("tries", {})
    for it in (it for it in load().values() if it.prose_only):
        while tries.get(it.id, 0) < TRIES and items.get(it.id, {}).get("score") is None:
            tries[it.id] = tries.get(it.id, 0) + 1
            try:
                items[it.id] = A.judge(it.id, ev, model)
            except OutOfCredit:
                raise
            except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - asked again; still missing, the page is incomplete
                print(f"[article] {out.name} {it.id}: FAILED {str(e)[:200]}", flush=True)
            _write(path, items)
    return items


def score_page(page: Path, data: list[Path], out: Path, model: str = MODEL, browsers: threading.Semaphore | None = None) -> dict:
    """Score the page in `page` (index.html, facts.json) made from `data`; see the module text."""
    path = out / "result.json"
    if path.exists():
        return _read(path, None)
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    ev = out / "evidence"
    if not (ev / "evidence.json").exists():
        with browsers or nullcontext():
            capture(str((page / "index.html").resolve()), ev, None, data)
    trust = _trust(page, ev, out, model)
    feedback = T.feedback(trust)
    rubric = {it.id: it for it in load().values() if it.scored}
    if trust["vetoed"]:
        result = {"score": 0.0, "vetoed": trust["vetoed"], "parts": {}, "complete": True,
                  "summary": "vetoed by " + ",".join(trust["vetoed"])}
    else:
        items = {**_judge(ev, out, model), **_article(ev, out, model)}
        parts = {k: items[k]["score"] for k in rubric if items.get(k, {}).get("score") is not None}
        for k, it in rubric.items():
            if k in parts:
                r = items[k]
                feedback.append(f"{k} {it.name}:{parts[k]:.2f}。{r.get('where') or ''} {r.get('reason') or ''}".strip())
        missing = [k for k in rubric if k not in parts]
        unchecked = trust["items"].get("1.3", {}).get("violated") is None
        weights = {k: WEIGHT.get(k, 1.0) for k in parts}
        result = {"score": sum(v * weights[k] for k, v in parts.items()) / sum(weights.values()) if parts else 0.0,
                  "vetoed": [], "parts": parts,
                  "complete": not missing and not unchecked,
                  "summary": " ".join(f"{k}={v:.2f}" for k, v in parts.items())
                             + (f"  unjudged {','.join(missing)}" if missing else "") + ("  1.3 unchecked" if unchecked else "")}
    e = _read(ev / "evidence.json", {})
    feedback.append(f"页面高 {e.get('page_height')}px,滚动截了 {len(e.get('frames', []))} 帧,"
                    f"滚动时固定在屏幕上的图 {sum(1 for c in e.get('scroll_story', []) if c['pinned'])} 张。")
    result["feedback"] = feedback
    _write(path, result)
    return result


def task_data(task: str) -> list[Path]:
    """A benchmark task's files, as a submission's writer finds them in data/."""
    return sorted((TASKS / task / "data").iterdir())

"""Data of the pudding.cool stories that published none, from each story's own GitHub repo.

    PYTHONPATH=src:../report-bench/src .venv/bin/python -m report_gepa.puddingrepo clone <cache_dir>/web <cache_dir>/repos
    PYTHONPATH=src:../report-bench/src .venv/bin/python -m report_gepa.puddingrepo pack <cache_dir>/repos data/pudding-repo

Most Pudding stories import their data at build time, so the page loads no data
file and report_gepa.puddingweb finds nothing: the table is inlined in a JS chunk.
The source data usually sits in the story's repo under the-pudding (src/data/,
static/assets/...). clone takes every story of puddingweb's summary.jsonl that
data/pudding-web has nothing for, looks for a public repo named after its slug
(also with _ for -), plus the repo OTHER names when the data sits elsewhere (the
page links to it), and shallow-clones them, checking out only their csv, tsv and
json files (no LFS objects), into <repos>/<slug>/ (the story's own) and
<repos>/<slug>--<owner>-<name>/ (another); <repos>/repos.jsonl
gets one line per story with the repos found.

pack keeps the csv and tsv files outside node_modules and .git, minus the
starter template's placeholders (test.csv, sample.csv, demo folders), and the
json lists of records as csv (puddingweb.records_csv). A file
whose contents data/pudding, data/pudding-web or an earlier file already has is
dropped (the copy a build puts in docs/ or public/), and a story is kept under
the same rule as puddingweb's pack: one of its files is a table of at least
MIN_ROWS rows and MIN_COLUMNS columns. The files go to <out>/<id>/ under their own
names (with their folders when two share a name) and <out>/manifest.jsonl gets
{id, title, url, repos, published, files, bytes}. These stories are for learning
and the benchmark only: report_gepa.optimize.split does not see them.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

from .optimize import DATA
from .puddingweb import KEEP, MIN_COLUMNS, MIN_ROWS, digest, manifest, records_csv, table_shape

WEB = DATA.parent / "pudding-web"
OWNER = "https://github.com/the-pudding/"
SKIP_DIRS = {".git", "node_modules", ".svelte-kit", "_records"}
OTHER = {  # story slug -> repo with its data, linked from the story page
    "love-songs": "the-pudding/pop-love-songs",
    "lenna": "the-pudding/lenna-data",
    "hamilton": "sxywu/hamilton",
    "asne": "googletrends/asne",
    "nba-moments": "googletrends/google_nba",
    "caption-contest": "nextml/caption-contest-data",
}
TEMPLATE = {"test.csv", "sample.csv", "demo-layercake.csv"}


def git(*args: str, timeout: int = 900) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    return subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout,
                          env={**os.environ, "GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE": "1"})


def clone(web: Path, repos: Path):
    repos.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    packed = {row["url"].rstrip("/").split("pudding.cool/")[-1] for row in manifest(WEB / "manifest.jsonl")}
    done = {row["url"] for row in manifest(repos / "repos.jsonl")}
    todo = [s for s in manifest(web / "summary.jsonl") if s["url"].rstrip("/") not in packed and s["url"] not in done]
    print(f"{len(todo)} stories to look up", flush=True)
    for s in todo:
        slug = s["url"].rstrip("/").split("/")[-1]
        own = next((name for name in dict.fromkeys([slug, slug.replace("-", "_")])
                    if git("ls-remote", "--heads", OWNER + name, timeout=60).returncode == 0), None)
        found = ([f"the-pudding/{own}"] if own else []) + ([OTHER[slug]] if slug in OTHER else [])
        for full in found:
            folder = repos / folder_name(slug, full)
            if not (folder / ".git").is_dir():
                # only the files pack reads: the rest of a story repo (images, audio, builds) is most of its size
                r = git("clone", "--depth", "1", "--single-branch", "--filter=blob:none", "--no-checkout",
                        f"https://github.com/{full}", str(folder))
                for step in (["sparse-checkout", "set", "--no-cone", "*.csv", "*.tsv", "*.json", "*.CSV", "*.TSV", "*.JSON"], ["checkout"]):
                    if r.returncode == 0:
                        r = git("-C", str(folder), *step)
                if r.returncode != 0:
                    print(f"{s['url']:40s} clone of {full} failed: {r.stderr.strip()[-200:]}", flush=True)
        with (repos / "repos.jsonl").open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps({"url": s["url"], "slug": slug, "title": s["title"], "repos": found}, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
        print(f"{s['url']:40s} {' '.join(found) or '-'}", flush=True)


def folder_name(slug: str, full: str) -> str:
    owner, name = full.split("/")
    return slug if owner == "the-pudding" and name in (slug, slug.replace("-", "_")) else f"{slug}--{owner}-{name}"


def tables(folder: Path) -> list[Path]:
    """The csv/tsv files first, then the json records, so a duplicate keeps the original csv."""
    found, records = [], []
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(folder):
        dirs[:] = sorted(d for d in dirs if d not in SKIP_DIRS and "demo" not in d.lower())
        found += [Path(root) / f for f in sorted(files) if Path(f).suffix.lower() in KEEP and f.lower() not in TEMPLATE]
        records += [Path(root) / f for f in sorted(files) if f.endswith(".json")]
    return found + [c for p in records if (c := records_csv(p))]


def pack(repos: Path, out: Path):
    seen = {digest(p) for d in (DATA, WEB) for p in d.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and p.suffix.lower() in KEEP}
    taken = {row["id"] for d in (DATA, WEB) for row in manifest(d / "manifest.jsonl")}
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)
